title: reCAPTCHA action mismatch: find and fix the pageAction
author: Bob
summary: The solver returns a token, the site takes it, and the request still fails with a generic "please try again". On reCAPTCHA v3 the usual cause is an action mismatch: the token was minted for one action and the site's backend expected another. If you leave pageAction out of the task, CapBypass mints the token for the action homepage , so a login form that checks for login will reject every token you send. Last week 0.8% of Enterprise v3 tasks arrived with no action at all. This post shows how to read the exact action off the page and the four ways it goes wrong. What an action mismatch looks like Every v3 token carries the action it was generated for. The site's backend verifies the token with Google and gets that action back. With classic keys it comes from siteverify : { "success" : true , "score" : 0.9 , "action" : "homepage" , "challenge_ts" : "2026-10-14T09:12:44Z" , "hostname" : "example.com" } Enterprise keys return it as tokenProperties.action in the assessment: { "tokenProperties" : { "valid" : true , "action" : "homepage" , "hostname" : "example.com" }, "riskAnalysis" : { "score" : 0.9 } } Note success: true and valid: true . Google says the token is genuine. It is the site's own code that compares action with what it expected ( login ) and refuses the request. That's why there is no error code for this, and why the response you see is whatever the site shows for any failed check. reCAPTCHA error codes covers the failures that do come with a code. Finding the action on the page The action is the second argument of the execute call: grecaptcha . execute ( ' 6LdyC2cUAAAAACGuDKpXeDorzUDWXmdqeg-xy696 ' , { action : ' login ' }) grecaptcha . enterprise . execute ( ' 6LcR... ' , { action : ' LOGIN ' }) Searching the page source for grecaptcha.execute( finds it on simple sites. Bundled apps build the options object somewhere else, so the search often lands on { action: e } . The faster route is to log the real value at runtime. Paste this in the DevTools console before you submit the form: for ( const api of [ window . grecaptcha , window . grecaptcha && window . grecaptcha . enterprise ]) { if ( ! api || ! api . execute ) continue ; const original = api . execute . bind ( api ); api . execute = ( key , opts ) => { console . log ( ' [recaptcha] key=%s action=%s ' , key , opts && opts . action ); return original ( key , opts ); }; } Now submit the form and read the console. If nothing prints, the app kept its own reference to execute before you patched it. Search the bundle for .execute( in the Sources tab (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+F), set a breakpoint on that line, submit again and read the action value when it pauses. Some pages call execute several times with different actions, one on page load ( homepage or pageview ) and one on submit. You want the one that fires right before the request you're automating. Sending the action with the task Pass the string exactly as logged, in pageAction : curl -s https://api.capbypass.pro/createTask \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "clientKey": "' " $CAPBYPASS_API_KEY " '", "task": { "type": "ReCaptchaV3TaskProxyLess", "websiteURL": "https://example.com/login", "websiteKey": "6LdyC2cUAAAAACGuDKpXeDorzUDWXmdqeg-xy696", "pageAction": "login" } }' The same with the Python SDK , which creates the task and polls it for you: import os from capbypass import CapBypass client = CapBypass ( api_key = os . environ [ " CAPBYPASS_API_KEY " ]) solution = client . solve ({ " type " : " ReCaptchaV3TaskProxyLess " , " websiteURL " : " https://example.com/login " , " websiteKey " : " 6LdyC2cUAAAAACGuDKpXeDorzUDWXmdqeg-xy696 " , " pageAction " : " login " , # exactly what grecaptcha.execute received }, timeout = 120 ) print ( solution [ " gRecaptchaResponse " ][: 40 ]) For an Enterprise key, change the type to ReCaptchaV3EnterpriseTaskProxyLess and keep the same field. If you run your own create/poll loop, the intervals and timeouts are in polling captcha API tasks . Bonus: +5% credits on every top-up New to CapBypass? Apply code WELCOME_2026 at checkout for an extra 5% in credits on every top-up, with no minimum and no expiry. Redeem it on the top-up page and put it toward your first ReCaptchaV3TaskProxyLess solves. The four mismatch patterns No action sent. The token is minted as homepage . This works only on pages whose own execute call uses homepage . Always send pageAction , even when you think the default fits. Wrong case or spelling. The comparison is a plain string match on the site's side, so Login , login and LOGIN are three different actions. Enterprise integrations often use upper case. Copy the logged value, don't retype it. Right action, wrong step. A checkout flow can run add_to_cart , checkout and purchase on the same page. Reusing the action from the first step on the last request fails. Match the action to the request that carries the token. Action built at runtime. Some apps derive it from the route or form id ( submit_contact , submit_newsletter ). Log it for each form you automate instead of assuming one value per site. Not an action problem, but often confused with one: a token older than 2 minutes or used twice. Google then reports timeout-or-duplicate and the site fails the same way. Solve right before the submit. Checking the fix If you own the site, log the action (or tokenProperties.action ) next to each verification result. One line per request settles the question in minutes. If you don't have the backend, compare the request the browser sends with yours in DevTools: same endpoint, same token field name, same action. Once the action matches and the request still fails, the problem is the score, not the action: why your reCAPTCHA v3 score is low walks through that side. All task fields are listed on the reCAPTCHA v3 docs page. Originally published on capbypass.pro . title: Building an Offline-First Crop Disease Detector with React Native, On-Device TFLite, and Grounded RAG
author: Keylor Pineda
summary: The Reality of Smallholder Agriculture in Central America In mountainous agricultural regions across Costa Rica and Central America, smallholder producers of coffee ( Coffea arabica ), cacao ( Theobroma cacao ), and banana ( Musa spp.) cultivate plots where cellular connectivity is intermittent or completely absent. When foliar and pod pathogens strike—such as Coffee Leaf Rust ( Hemileia vastatrix ), Cacao Frosty Pod Rot ( Moniliophthora roreri ), or Banana Black Sigatoka ( Pseudocercospora fijiensis )—early and accurate diagnosis is critical. A delay of several days or a mistaken treatment can destroy an entire seasonal harvest. Cloud-based computer vision APIs fail in this environment: when standing in a steep coffee parcel miles away from the nearest cell tower, an app requiring a round-trip network request is unusable. To address this challenge, we built HealthyCropping , an open-source, non-commercial, offline-first Android application. GitHub Repository: https://github.com/keylorpineda/healthycropping Architectural Principle: 100% Offline by Default HealthyCropping was architected so that no core user action—capturing a photo, running deep learning inference, evaluating disease severity, or registering a plot sector—requires an internet connection. Field Camera Capture: Guided framing tips tailored to leaf underside (coffee/banana) or pod surface (cacao). On-Device Preprocessing: In-memory 224x224 RGB decoding and normalization. Offline Inference: MobileNetV3 TFLite models running locally in under 50ms. Instant Severity Triage: Results reported immediately on screen with actionable status (healthy, watch, act now). Local Persistence: Data written to expo-sqlite using client-side UUIDs. Optional Cloud Bridge: Asynchronous batch synchronization with FastAPI and Gemini RAG once connectivity is restored. Challenge 1: Edge Inference Without Freezing the UI Thread Running deep learning models on mid-range and low-end Android hardware presents severe memory and latency constraints. Loading a full TensorFlow runtime or converting uncompressed models causes dropped frames, out-of-memory crashes, and excessive battery drain. We addressed this through three key architectural decisions: Specialist Models per Plant Organ: Instead of an oversized multi-class model trying to classify all plants at once, we trained dedicated MobileNetV3-Large architectures focused on specific plant organs: Coffee Leaf, Cacao Pod, and Banana Leaf. Quantization: Models are exported and quantized to float16 and INT8, reducing file sizes to below 10 MB per model. Hardware Acceleration via Fast TFLite: We utilize react-native-fast-tflite, which binds directly to native C++ TFLite runtimes using GPU/NNAPI delegates where available. On test hardware, inference consistently completes in under 50 milliseconds . Challenge 2: The Tensor Parity Trap A common pitfall in edge machine learning is training-to-deployment preprocessing drift . A model trained in Python with Keras might achieve 95% accuracy on test splits, but once deployed in a mobile JavaScript environment, slight differences in image decoding, resizing interpolation, or RGB normalization formulas degrade real-world accuracy drastically. To prevent this drift, we created a shared fixture test suite between the Python ML repository ( ml/ ) and the React Native client ( app/ ): A reference test image is passed through Python preprocessing ( ml/src/preprocessing/ ). The resulting 224x224 RGB float array is exported as an exact numerical fixture. A Jest unit test in React Native runs the mobile decoding pipeline ( app/src/ml/preprocessor.ts ) and asserts bit-for-bit parity against the Python reference tensor. If any change is made to normalization statistics or channel ordering, the automated CI pipeline fails before any model reaches the mobile bundle. Challenge 3: Offline Data Integrity with SQLite Farms, plots, and scans are stored locally using expo-sqlite . Because users work offline for days, primary keys cannot rely on auto-incrementing database IDs generated by a remote server. We generate client-side UUIDv4 identifiers for all entities. When connectivity is eventually restored, an idempotent synchronization engine reconciles local changes with our remote backend: Unsynced records are batched into a single payload. The backend processes records with upsert semantics, eliminating duplicate entries caused by network drops during sync. Challenge 4: Preventing Dangerous AI Hallucinations Generative AI in agriculture presents a serious risk: an unconstrained Large Language Model might invent chemical mixtures, incorrect dosages, or illegal fungicides that harm crops, contaminate soil, or void organic certifications. HealthyCropping uses a Grounded Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline powered by FastAPI and Gemini: Curated Agronomic Corpus: We ingest verified technical manuals from national institutions (such as Costa Rica's ICAFE for coffee and CATIE for cacao). Strict Source Attribution: The RAG prompt strictly confines Gemini to the retrieved manual passages. It is instructed to reject answering if verified guidance is missing. Structured Recommendations: Guidance is categorized into Cultural Controls (e.g., pruning, shade regulation) and Approved Phytosanitary Measures, always citing the exact manual title and page number. Current Status and Open Source Opportunities HealthyCropping is actively in development across 9 structured phases: Phases 1 to 5 (Completed): Model pipelines for coffee, cacao, and banana; float16/INT8 TFLite export; Expo React Native client shell; offline SQLite schema; and camera triage interface. Phases 6 and 7 (In Progress): FastAPI cloud synchronization, Firebase token boundaries, Cloudinary image ingestion, and Gemini RAG advisory integration. We welcome open-source contributions across all layers: Mobile Engineers (React Native, TypeScript, Expo, SQLite): Sync engine optimizations, battery profiling, and UI testing. Backend Engineers (Python 3.12, FastAPI, Firebase Admin): Batch sync endpoints, async processing pipelines, and API security. ML Engineers (TensorFlow, TFLite): Quantization-aware training (QAT), dataset validation, and mobile inference benchmarks. Agronomists & Researchers: Manual curation, retrieval chunk validation, and field trial feedback. Explore the Code GitHub Repository: https://github.com/keylorpineda/healthycropping Architecture Overview: https://github.com/keylorpineda/healthycropping/blob/develop/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md Implementation Roadmap: https://github.com/keylorpineda/healthycropping/blob/develop/docs/PLAN.md Contributing Guidelines: https://github.com/keylorpineda/healthycropping/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md Feedback, issues, and discussions are welcome.

title: Hornet: A Local Coding Goal You Can Inspect, Pause, and Resume
author: Daniel
summary: A useful coding run should leave more than a convincing final message. It should leave changed files, checks you can examine, and enough saved state to understand what happened if the process stops. That is the problem Hornet addresses. It gives a local model a coding goal, organizes the work into small scoped cells, and keeps the goal, attempts, questions, and execution evidence on disk. This walkthrough uses Hornet 0.15.1 , Python 3.13 on Windows , LM Studio , and a new Ubuntu worker VM in VirtualBox . We will repair one Python function, inspect the result, and see how to return to unfinished work. The commands follow the release’s starter walkthrough; the live-model measurements later in this article come from the separately documented 0.15.0 trial. Hornet was created and is led by Daniel F. MacDonald , with engineering contributions credited in the project. It is available under AGPL-3.0-only . Source and current documentation Installable PyPI release: matrixswarm-hornet 0.15.1 Signed starter release What a durable coding goal contains Hornet separates the saved work from the model’s current working context. A coding cell has an explicit task, permitted files, an expected result with a declared type, acceptance checks, and execution limits. The controller records those commitments, runs the work, and checks the result before accepting completion. Larger goals can be divided into ordered cells within configured limits; this first exercise deliberately uses one. The active request contains bounded context and references to retained evidence. Source is read as needed. Earlier exchanges can leave the active request while their full records remain available on disk. This limits what each request carries without treating an old failure as if it never happened. Situation What Hornet retains or does An attempt fails Keeps its conditions, errors, and verification evidence The model needs a decision Saves a question and waits for an explicit answer The controller is interrupted Uses checkpoints and operation receipts to assess whether work can resume A goal completes Keeps its workspace and exports candidate changes for review A finished file needs a follow-up Creates a revision workspace that records its parent The current workers and model roles run sequentially . A plan with multiple cells is not a claim that several models are working concurrently. The detailed behavior is documented in the CLI reference . 1. Prepare the host and obtain the starter For the documented path, have these installed on Windows: Python 3.13, available through the Python launcher; VirtualBox and Windows OpenSSH; LM Studio and a model compatible with the request protocol used below; GnuPG, such as Gpg4win, for release verification. Allow one CPU, 2 GiB of RAM, and disk space for the Ubuntu image and worker VM. Those are the worker’s requirements; the local model needs its own host memory and compute capacity. The arrangement is straightforward: Windows host Hornet controller → LM Studio on 127.0.0.1:1234 │ └── pinned SSH on 127.0.0.1:2224 │ dedicated Ubuntu VM model-requested file and code operations The model stays on the host. Its requested coding operations run inside the VM. This walkthrough uses Hornet’s own CLI and worker setup. From the v0.15.1 release , download the starter ZIP , checksum manifest, detached signature, public signing key, and verification instructions. The named starter includes an installable wheel and setup helpers. GitHub’s automatic source ZIP is a different download and does not contain that wheel. Follow VERIFY-RELEASE.md before extracting the starter: Inspect the public key and compare the complete primary fingerprint with a trusted, independently obtained MatrixSwarm release identity. Verify the detached signature over SHA256SUMS and check the expected signing identity. Match the downloaded files against the authenticated SHA-256 manifest. The supplied all-files verification loop expects the files named in that manifest to be present. Extract the verified starter into a new directory. The published primary fingerprint is: 8086 C2A9 440B 9226 FA7A 78E5 BC01 80CF 9A93 5966 A key and a checksum obtained from the same download location provide a consistency check; that alone does not independently establish who owns the key. The verification guide explains this distinction and supplies the exact GnuPG and PowerShell commands. 2. Install Hornet and check a local file contract Open PowerShell in the extracted starter directory . Keep that working directory for the commands in this article. The following path installs the wheel included in the signed starter into a fresh Python 3.13 environment: py -3 . 13 -m venv . venv . \.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --no-index --no-deps . \matrixswarm_hornet-0.15.1-py3-none-any.whl . \.venv\Scripts\hornet.exe --version . \.venv\Scripts\python.exe . \tools\first_run.py --project . \my-first-goal Look for: matrixswarm-hornet 0.15.1 INSTALLATION CHECK PASSED The commands call the environment’s executable directly. There is no need to activate a PowerShell script or change script execution policy. The first-run helper creates a new project, runs local diagnostics, and writes a small hello.txt file. It then verifies a contract requiring that file to exist, contain the expected text, and meet a minimum size. It also copies the coding goal into the project for the next steps. This check uses no model and no worker . It establishes that the installed CLI and local contract path work. It does not establish that LM Studio or the VM is ready. The helper refuses to overwrite an existing project; use a fresh directory for another trial. The PyPI installation option Hornet is also installable from PyPI: python -m pip install matrixswarm-hornet python -m hornet --version python -m hornet --help Run those commands inside the Python environment you intend to use. For a version-pinned reproduction of this article, select matrixswarm-hornet==0.15.1 . Choose one installation route. The remaining commands below use the starter’s .venv created above. Installing through an unrelated global python will not populate that environment, and the PyPI package alone does not supply this extracted starter directory’s VM-setup layout. The package supports Python 3.9 and later and has no runtime Python dependencies. We use 3.13 to match the documented first-user setup. PyPI’s embedded README reflects the uploaded release snapshot; use the current GitHub README for current installation prose. 3. Create a new dedicated worker VM Use the Ubuntu 22.04 AMD64 cloud VMDK from the official Jammy cloud-image directory . Obtain its checksum manifest and signature, establish trust in that manifest, and use the full SHA-256 for the exact VMDK downloaded. Do not substitute an ISO, an OVA, or a checksum from a different daily image. The documented validation used the October 20, 2026 image; a newer image is a different input and is not covered by that particular trial. The worker setup expects Python 3, Git, and OpenSSH server in the image. It does not silently upgrade the guest or install missing guest packages. See the complete worker setup guide for image and provisioning details. Install the setup-only ISO-building dependency, then supply your image path and verified checksum: . \.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install pycdlib == 1.14 . 0 $image = 'C:\Downloads\jammy-server-cloudimg-amd64.vmdk' $imageHash = 'PASTE_THE_FULL_SHA256_FOR_THAT_IMAGE' $vmFolder = Join-Path $ env : USERPROFILE 'VirtualBox VMs' . \.venv\Scripts\python.exe . \tools\prepare_worker.py --project . \my-first-goal --image $image --image-sha256 $imageHash --vm-parent $vmFolder --name hornet-first-goal --port 2224 Replace the image path and hash placeholders. Choose an unused VM name and loopback port. The helper creates a new worker; it does not adopt an existing VM or overwrite an established worker configuration. During setup it generates fresh SSH keys, pins the worker’s host key, restricts the local private directory, and binds SSH forwarding to loopback. Shared folders, shared clipboard, and drag-and-drop are not enabled. The VM uses NAT and has outbound networking. The guest hornet account has no sudo access. Its SSH key is restricted to the worker entry point, but the model can still request Python execution as that guest user. The dedicated VM supplies the execution boundary. Separate goal directories share its account; they are not separate sandboxes for hostile code. Keep unrelated secrets out of the VM. Wait for the first boot, then check readiness: . \.venv\Scripts\hornet.exe --root . \my-first-goal worker-status --worker-config worker.json --json Proceed when the result shows ready: true . An early connection refusal can mean the VM is still starting. A persistent failure calls for inspecting its console and cloud-init output. A host-key mismatch requires checking the saved identity, not disabling verification. The generated my-first-goal/private/ directory contains the SSH identity, host-key material, and seed ISO. Retain it for this worker and exclude it from Git and uploads. 4. Connect the local model Load a compatible model in LM Studio, open its Developer tab, and start the local server. LM Studio documents this in its local server guide . For the endpoint used by the starter, inspect the available model IDs: Invoke-RestMethod http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1/models | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 6 Set $model to the exact ID returned for your chosen model. The documented Gemma example uses: $model = 'google/gemma-4-12b' Use that value only if it is the model your server actually exposes. The starter uses lmstudio-json , a constrained-JSON request mode; a server being generally OpenAI-compatible does not guarantee it supports every option this mode needs. The CLI documentation records testing with LM Studio 0.4.26 and that Gemma model. Model behavior and speed will vary. 5. Give it one precise coding goal The starter’s calculator.py deliberately returns its input: def double ( n ): """ Return twice an integer (the starter intentionally needs a repair). """ return n There is a useful trap here: the existing tests check the integer return type and the zero case. This incorrect function can pass those tests. A green test suite is only as informative as the behavior it exercises. The supplied demo-goal.txt makes the missing behavior explicit: Fix calculator.py so double(n) returns 2*n for an integer n, with an integer return type. Required examples: double(-3) == -6, double(0) == 0, double(7) == 14. Only calculator.py may change. Preserve its public function name and argument. Keep the existing tests unchanged. Use one coding cell and verify the required behavior. That gives the run a small file scope, concrete examples, a return-type requirement, and a constraint against solving the task by rewriting the existing tests. Start the goal with the documented limits: . \.venv\Scripts\hornet.exe --root . \my-first-goal autowork --worker-config worker.json --goal-file demo-goal.txt --model $model --base-url http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1 --protocol lmstudio-json --max-cells 1 --max-turns 30 --max-tools 40 --cell-turns 10 --cell-tools 16 --context-chars 16000 --max-tokens 2048 --timeout 120 --json The command is long because its limits are explicit: Setting Meaning in this exercise --max-cells 1 Keep the plan to one coding cell --max-turns 30 , --max-tools 40 Bound model requests and tool operations across the goal --cell-turns 10 , --cell-tools 16 Bound the individual coding cell --context-chars 16000 Bound active working context in characters --max-tokens 2048 Cap a model response’s output tokens --timeout 120 Set the socket-operation timeout; not an overall completion deadline The context setting is a character budget, not a token count or a change to the model’s loaded context window. Backend framing adds overhead. Use the recorded usage to assess the actual run. Hornet prepares a separate goal workspace in the VM. Planning and verification roles establish checks before coding, and the controller keeps the frozen checks outside the worker’s editable source. It requires new source changes, the suite, and the applicable cell and goal checks before reporting completion. For this autonomous goal, success means completed , with the coding cell ready_for_review . A zero process exit, waiting_for_user , or paused is not equivalent to completed coding work. 6. Inspect the changed source and saved evidence Save the exact run_dir returned by the command: $run = 'PASTE_THE_EXACT_RUN_DIR_FROM_THE_RESULT' . \.venv\Scripts\hornet.exe --root . \my-first-goal goal-files $run . \.venv\Scripts\hornet.exe --root . \my-first-goal questions $run Use that run’s paths rather than guessing the newest directory. goal-files connects file hashes, cell identities, changes, and revision provenance; it rebuilds this view from validated evidence. There are two locations to understand: Inside the VM: each autonomous goal has its own source directory under /home/hornet/workspace/goals/ , with its generated workspace ID. The original worker baseline remains separate. On the controller: the project retains the run directory, normally beneath my-first-goal/coding/recipes/ , containing its goal, checkpoints, cell jobs, results, and evidence. Within the reported run, the useful records include: Record What to inspect goal.json and goal-acceptance.json Original requirements and frozen overall checks recipe-checkpoint.json Saved execution phase, source state, and counters goal-status.json Derived progress and outcome view file-index.json File hashes and the cells responsible for them cells/<cell-id>/return-manifest.json Declared result, changed-file hashes, and references to checks and attempts cells/<cell-id>/jobs/<job-run>/changes.json Exported changed-file content and tracked diff The job’s verification/ and attempts/ directories Verification rounds and retained attempt evidence goal-completion.json Links the completed goal to its source state, receipts, and final evidence Open the calculator.py entry in the job’s changes.json : its content field contains the exported source. Compare it with the starter and read the recorded diff. Confirm that only the allowed file changed and that the function handles the required examples while preserving its interface. For this exercise, a minimal repair is to preserve the function and return 2 * n . Inspect the actual exported implementation rather than assuming it took that form. The resulting behavior should be: Call Required result double(-3) -6 double(0) 0 double(7) 14 Read the assertions as well as their verdicts. Hornet can verify that checks ran and that declared result types matched; a model-authored assertion can still misunderstand the task. Exported work remains a candidate for your review, with integration into your own source as a separate step. 7. Answer a saved question or resume unfinished work If the run returns waiting_for_user , list its questions with the command above. Copy the exact question ID and answer that question: . \.venv\Scripts\hornet.exe --root . \my-first-goal answer $run q-EXACT_ID --text 'Your answer' . \.venv\Scripts\hornet.exe --root . \my-first-goal autoresume $run --json Replace both placeholders with the actual run and a substantive answer. Saving the answer does not start execution. autoresume explicitly continues the autonomous goal. While a required question waits, the controller process can exit. There is no response deadline or repeated model inference consuming resources while you are away. Resuming without an answer keeps the work waiting. The question is allowed to be more patient than a chat window. Use autoresume for an interrupted autonomous goal too. Standalone work jobs use resume instead. A completed goal is not unfinished work to resume; use a revision for a new request. Keep the project, run evidence, worker keys, VM, and source intact. Resume checks identities and saved source state before continuing. For supported worker operations, durable receipts can resolve a lost reply when the operation and its completed result match. A started operation without a completed receipt remains uncertain. Hornet stops for inspection instead of assuming it is safe to repeat. This supports recovery from specific interruptions; it does not promise exactly-once effects in external systems or universal recovery from every power loss. 8. Make a targeted revision and retain the parent After the first goal completes, a small follow-up is: . \.venv\Scripts\hornet.exe --root . \my-first-goal revise $run --file calculator.py --goal 'Add triple(n) returning 3*n for integers. Preserve double(n).' A revision creates another workspace and records the parent. It selects the requested file scope and declared dependencies, then uses new checks and retained regression checks. Inspect the revision’s own result and run directory just as you did for the original. Declared dependencies are not a complete static analysis of every consumer in a codebase. Start with a scope you can review. After the controller exits, you can shut down the demo VM through VirtualBox’s ACPI mechanism: & 'C:\Program Files\Oracle\VirtualBox\VBoxManage.exe' controlvm hornet-first-goal acpipowerbutton Restart the same retained VM before resume or revision: & 'C:\Program Files\Oracle\VirtualBox\VBoxManage.exe' startvm hornet-first-goal --type headless Adjust the executable path and VM name if you chose different ones. Shutting down the worker preserves it; deleting it would remove part of the saved working environment. What has actually been validated The published validation record reports an earlier 0.15.0 live trial on a fresh Python 3.13 environment, on an existing Windows host, with a newly provisioned Ubuntu 22.04 VM and Gemma 12B: Observation Recorded result Model requests 16 Tool calls 5 Peak input 3,084 tokens Changed source Only calculator.py Independent behavior checks [-6, 0, 14] Original worker baseline Preserved These are observations from one deliberately small goal. They are not a general reliability benchmark, a speed promise, or a prediction of another model’s request count. For 0.15.1 , the release work added packaging, publication metadata, license, documentation, and distribution checks. The executable baseline and demo were retained apart from the version string. The publication record reports that the PyPI and TestPyPI files match the original signed GitHub artifacts, with fresh installation, version, and first-goal file-contract checks passing on Windows Python 3.13 and an Ubuntu workflow runner. The PyPI publication workflow records the successful verification. Those publication checks did not run a new live-model benchmark. Keeping that distinction visible makes the evidence more useful. title: Jev: what it's for and how to use it
author: Ilia
summary: A message arrives in a chat: “How can I enable notifications for new orders only?” The application needs to assign it a category: “question”, “advertising”, or “other”. The category determines what happens next. Jev from TypeSafe AI takes data and typed questions, then returns values your code can use: a label, a score on a scale, or the probability of a “yes” answer. General LLMs also support structured outputs, so you can build a similar workflow with them. Jev is worth considering when you want an API contract built around decisions: probabilities across predefined options and independent questions about the same data in one call. Your application gets both a result and probability estimates it can use to choose its next action. This walkthrough follows the API documentation as of October 22, 2026. I haven't called the service or tested its probability calibration, accuracy, or speed for this article. A category, a scale, or a yes/no question Three question types are useful for text tasks. Choice selects one option from a set, such as “question”, “advertising”, or “other” for a chat message. You could also classify a support request by topic and route it to the right handler: billing, shipping, or returns. The categories have no inherent order. Score rates text against ordered levels. For a support queue, you could describe urgency as “can wait”, “disrupts work, but a workaround exists”, and “work has stopped”. Those three levels occupy positions 0 through 2. The resulting score can fall between levels, so it may be fractional. It represents a position on the scale you described. Noul returns the probability of a “yes” answer as a number from 0 to 1. For example, you could ask whether a comment contains personal data or whether a customer wants to speak to a person. This signal can help with moderation or a handoff to a human agent; your application sets the threshold for taking action. In one call, you could use Choice to classify a message and Noul to check whether it contains personal data. The application gets both a category and an additional signal for review. Each question is evaluated independently: the second does not receive the first one's answer. Your code needs to handle any dependencies between decisions. Your first request: classify a message We'll use Choice with the categories “question”, “advertising”, and “other”. The instructions will define a rule for mixed cases: if a promotional message contains a question, classify it as advertising. The quickstart requires Python 3.10 or later and the official typesafe-sdk package. Get an API key from the TypeSafe console and set the TYPESAFE_API_KEY environment variable. In a POSIX shell: python3 -m pip install typesafe-sdk export TYPESAFE_API_KEY = "your-api-key" Save the following code as classify_message.py . The client reads the key from the environment. Following the documentation's example, jev-latest selects the current model without pinning a version. from typesafe_sdk import Choice , TypeSafeClient message = " How can I enable notifications for new orders only? " with TypeSafeClient ( model = " jev-latest " ) as client : response = client . system_one ( state = message , questions = { " message_type " : Choice ( instructions = ( " Classify this chat message. " " If a promotional message contains a question, choose advertising. " ), criteria = { " question " : " A request for help or information without advertising " , " advertising " : " Promotion of a product, service, or external channel " , " other " : " Neither advertising nor a request for help or information " , }, ), }, ) answer = response . choices [ " message_type " ] print ( " Label: " , answer . choice ) print ( " Probabilities: " , answer . probabilities ) print ( " Confidence: " , answer . confidence ) Run python3 classify_message.py in the same shell session. state contains the text to evaluate. It can also hold structured data, such as a message together with the chat's rules. In questions , the message_type identifier links the question to its answer, instructions defines the task, and criteria describes the categories. The Python SDK makes Choice answers available through response.choices . The .choice field holds the label with the highest probability; .probabilities holds the distribution across the options. If “question” and “advertising” have similar probabilities, your application can send the message for review even though one label has technically won. The distribution lets your code account for that ambiguity when choosing an action. For Choice, confidence is calculated from the highest probability, adjusted for the number of options. A uniform distribution gives 0; assigning all probability to one option gives 1. It is a separate measure from the probability of the selected label. Even a high value does not guarantee that the model understood the message correctly. Jev fits application steps that turn text into a predefined decision: choosing a handler, setting priorities, or flagging a message for a moderator. After classification, a message labeled as a question can go to a bot that drafts a reply. Generating a detailed response or doing extended reasoning requires a separate step; Jev sits between the input data and your code's next action.

title: Do AI Coding Agents Need a Different CSS Architecture?
author: Marvin Ahlgrimm
summary:
Does BEM Still Make Sense When AI Writes CSS? I use BEM. Sometimes. Most of my CSS is plain CSS, with a main stylesheet and a few additional files for specific areas, such as blog.css . The HTML is rendered on the server using Marten . During deployment, a minifier takes care of the CSS, and Marten's collectassets handles fingerprinting. That's pretty much my entire CSS toolchain. And I like it. There's very little overhead, and it does everything I currently need. But with AI coding agents writing more of my code, I started wondering whether my approach still made sense. Should I use BEM more consistently? Switch to data attributes for modifiers? Or consider something like Tailwind or CSS Modules? I ended up asking a Codex agent whether replacing BEM modifiers with data-* attributes would improve an existing project. Its answer was rather simple: data-* doesn't automatically make sense as a replacement for BEM modifiers. Well, that wasn't quite the answer I expected. But it got me thinking. Maybe the more important question isn't which CSS methodology an agent should use, but how to make sure it understands the decisions already made in a project. BEM, modifiers, and data attributes Here's a typical BEM example:

Hello World

A short description.

I like how predictable this is. The relationship between the elements is obvious, and I don't have to worry too much about a generic .title selector affecting something elsewhere. That's useful when working with global CSS. Of course, BEM doesn't actually isolate styles. It relies on naming conventions to avoid collisions. And I don't think every simple layout needs a complete BEM structure. But what about modifiers? Instead of: I could write: I actually prefer the second version here. The attributes make it clear that variant and size are independent properties. Modern CSS handles this quite nicely: .button { padding : 0.5rem 1rem ; &:where([data-variant="primary"]) { background : var ( --color-primary ); color : white ; } & :where ([ data-size = "large" ]) { padding : 0.75rem 1.5rem ; } } Using :where() prevents the attribute condition from adding specificity. Without it, .button[data-variant="primary"] would be more specific than .button--primary . So far, so good. But Codex had a point. Compare:
With:
What exactly do I gain by replacing the first with the second? Not much, especially if the existing modifier is already understood throughout the project. I still like data attributes for components with multiple named variants. But changing working code just because another syntax looks a little cleaner doesn't seem particularly useful. Do we need the modifier at all? The Codex agent also raised a more useful point: if a component already exposes its state through a semantic attribute, why introduce another representation just for styling? Imagine an accordion trigger: Now we have three representations of the same state. The BEM modifier says it's open, the data attribute says it's open, and aria-expanded says it's open. Why? For an ordinary disclosure component, I could avoid this entirely by using native HTML:
Details

Some additional information.

.accordion :where ([ open ]) > .accordion__trigger { font-weight : bold ; } The browser already manages the open state. And if I need several disclosure elements where only one can be open at a time, the name attribute on
can handle that too. Not every accordion or disclosure interface fits the native element, of course. For a custom implementation, aria-expanded may still be necessary. In that case, I can use it directly for styling: .accordion__trigger :where ([ aria-expanded = "true" ]) { /* Expanded styles */ } Now there's less state to keep synchronized. The same applies to disabled buttons. HTML already has disabled , and CSS provides :disabled . There's no reason to invent another representation of that state. This doesn't mean adding ARIA attributes just for styling. They still need to describe the interface correctly. And data-* remains useful for custom states that don't have an appropriate native or ARIA representation. But before introducing another modifier, it's worth checking whether HTML already provides what we need. Would another CSS methodology help? I also looked beyond BEM and data attributes. CSS Modules, Tailwind, CUBE CSS, ITCSS, and other approaches offer different ways to organize or write styles. But for my setup, only a few seem particularly relevant. CSS Modules CSS Modules solves one of BEM's problems differently: instead of relying on globally unique class names, it scopes them during the build. That's attractive. Classes like .title or .icon can be local to a component without requiring a naming convention. But I'd also need a transformation step and a way to use the generated class mappings in my Marten templates. If I were already using a component-based frontend with a build pipeline, CSS Modules would be an obvious candidate. For my current setup, I don't have enough problems with class collisions to justify adding that integration. Tailwind CSS I initially associated Tailwind with a much larger frontend toolchain. That wasn't entirely fair. Tailwind's CLI can compile static CSS during a build, without requiring React, Vite, or JavaScript in the browser. Adding it to my Containerfile wouldn't necessarily be difficult. The bigger difference is how I'd work with CSS. Instead of writing component styles separately, I'd compose utilities directly in the markup. I can see why that's useful, including for AI agents. Tailwind provides a predefined vocabulary rather than leaving every class name up to the developer or agent. But I still prefer meaningful component classes over long utility lists in my templates. And Tailwind has conventions of its own, such as making sure its source scanner can detect the utility classes being used. I'm not convinced that switching would make my development workflow better. It would mostly make it different. CUBE CSS CUBE CSS is probably the approach I found most relevant to my existing setup. It separates Composition, Utility, Block, and Exception. I particularly like the distinction between layout composition and component styling. Unlike CSS Modules or Tailwind, I can borrow these ideas without changing my toolchain. I can keep my stylesheets, use BEM-style names where they make sense, and organize the CSS a little more deliberately. And CSS itself? Part of the reason I'm comfortable keeping vanilla CSS is how much the language has improved. Nesting, custom properties, container queries, cascade layers, and @scope all address problems that previously required additional conventions or tooling. For example, cascade layers let me explicitly define the precedence of different groups of styles: @layer base , components , utilities ; And @scope lets me target elements within a particular part of the DOM without relying entirely on globally unique selectors. It's now supported in current versions of the major browsers, although older browser support still matters. It isn't the same kind of isolation as CSS Modules either. None of these features replaces BEM, but they give me more options for solving specific problems without introducing another toolchain. What actually changed with AI? After looking into these approaches, I couldn't find convincing evidence that AI agents produce more maintainable CSS with BEM, Tailwind, CSS Modules, or data attributes. Each has plausible advantages. Tailwind provides a shared vocabulary. CSS Modules offers local class scoping. BEM makes naming patterns predictable. But I don't think we can conclude that one is inherently better for AI-assisted development. What matters more to me is consistency. If an agent works on a component that already uses BEM, it shouldn't introduce data attributes just because they look more modern. If a component already exposes its state through aria-expanded , it shouldn't add data-state to represent the same thing. And if the project already has design tokens, it shouldn't invent a slightly different color or spacing value for every new component. So rather than replacing my CSS architecture, I've been making its conventions more explicit. For one of my projects, I put the UI guidance into a repository-local Codex skill under .agents/skills/ . The skill describes existing components, where shared design tokens belong, how variants and UI states should be handled, and which stylesheets to look at. It also points to the component gallery, so an agent has actual examples rather than just abstract rules. The relevant conventions can be summarized as: ## Component styling - Follow existing component and CSS conventions. - Reuse shared design tokens. - Check existing components before creating new ones. - Preserve clear BEM-style names. - Use native HTML states where appropriate. - Reuse semantically correct ARIA states for styling. - Avoid duplicating state across classes and attributes. - Use data attributes when they make variants clearer. These are the principles rather than a verbatim extract from the skill. In AGENTS.md , a short reference is enough: For changes to UI templates, CSS, or visual Stimulus states, use the repository-local UI skill. I like this separation. The agent has access to detailed UI guidance when it's relevant, without loading all of it for unrelated backend work. It's not a new CSS architecture. It's a way to make the existing one easier to understand and continue. Of course, the skill doesn't guarantee correct code. I still have to review what the agent produces. But it reduces how much of the project's styling conventions I have to explain repeatedly. And perhaps that's where AI has changed my approach the most. Decisions that previously lived in my head now benefit from being documented somewhere an agent can find them. So, is BEM still worth using? For me, yes. I don't see a reason to replace my current CSS setup. It's comfortable, requires very little maintenance, and works well for the applications I'm building. I'll continue using BEM where it makes sense, use data attributes when they add clarity, and take advantage of modern CSS features when they solve an actual problem. There's also plenty to learn from approaches like CUBE CSS without adopting an entirely new system. But the most useful result of this research wasn't discovering a better naming convention. It was making the conventions I already use more explicit. And I still find it amusing that the Codex agent, which prompted me to question my CSS approach in the first place, ended up arguing against changing it just for the sake of change. I think I'll take its advice on this one.

title: How to Scope and Price an HVAC Contractor Website
author: Amanur Rahman
summary: If you build sites for local service businesses, HVAC contractors are a good client type and an easy one to underprice. Their sites look like brochure sites, but the features that matter are closer to a small web app. Here is how I scope and price them. Why HVAC is not a standard brochure site Three things change the work: Two visitor types. One person has a dead furnace tonight and wants a phone number. The other is planning a replacement and wants proof and financing. The site must serve both in seconds. Seasonality. Cooling and heating messaging swap through the year, so the homepage needs content that is easy to change. Back-office links. Many contractors run dispatch or scheduling software, so forms and booking often need to connect to it. Typical price ranges (US-style market) Build route Typical upfront cost DIY builder $0 to $300 Template WordPress by a freelancer $1,200 to $3,000 Custom WordPress by an experienced freelancer $3,000 to $7,500 Agency $7,500 to $25,000+ Most single-location companies that want a site that books jobs fall in the $3,000 to $7,000 band. Line items to quote separately Feature Typical add-on Sticky click-to-call and emergency banner $100 to $300 Service pages $100 to $300 each City pages with unique local content $75 to $250 each Booking or request-a-visit form $400 to $1,500 Maintenance-plan sign-up with recurring billing $800 to $2,500 Financing link or embed $200 to $800 Dispatch software connection $500 to $2,000 Speed and basic SEO setup $500 to $1,500 Splitting the quote this way stops scope creep, because the client can see what each request costs. The feature worth getting right Maintenance plans. They are a membership or subscription build, and on WordPress they run on the same recurring-payment tools online stores use: plan tiers, renewal emails, receipts and a small account area. It adds real recurring revenue for the client, which makes the price easy to justify. Where scoping goes wrong Thin city pages. Swapping a town name in a template does not rank. Start with three to six towns and write each with real local detail. Skipping maintenance. Without updates the site slows down and becomes insecure. Quote a monthly plan up front. Launch timing. Work back from the client's busy season. Launch the essentials first and add city pages in a second phase if needed. FAQ Is WordPress a good fit for HVAC sites? Yes. It handles service pages, many city pages, memberships and booking connections, and the client owns the site. How long does a custom build take? Roughly four to nine weeks. Client content, like photos and service details, is the usual cause of delays. What are the ongoing costs? Hosting and maintenance usually total $65 to $310 per month. Scheduling or dispatch software is separate and often larger. Should I use a builder instead? For a new one-truck business, maybe. Recurring plans, booking connections and many location pages get awkward on builders. title: Testimonials with real consent: a data model for permission you can prove and revoke
author: Nazma Akter
summary: "Best candle I've ever bought." A customer quote is only worth putting on your homepage if the customer said you could, and only as long as they still agree. In ProofLoom testimonials are built around that rule. The one-minute reel shows the flow from the customer's side and the owner's. Here's how the data model keeps it honest. 1. One link, used anywhere A collection link is a public form at /review/<form_id> . The owner can send it straight to customers or put it on any page as a "Write a review" button. The form has a hidden honeypot field, and the same text sent to the same form within a short window is treated as a duplicate instead of a second testimonial. 2. Permissions are separate columns, and paid ads can't be granted Every grant is a row in testimonial_consents : website_publication BOOLEAN NOT NULL , social_publication BOOLEAN NOT NULL , name_display BOOLEAN NOT NULL , avatar_display BOOLEAN NOT NULL , paid_advertising BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false CHECK ( paid_advertising = false ), wording_version TEXT NOT NULL , evidence_source TEXT NOT NULL CHECK ( evidence_source IN ( 'customer_form' , 'owner_attested' )), granted_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now (), revoked_at TIMESTAMPTZ There's no single "I agree" flag. The paid_advertising column exists for the audit trail, and a CHECK constraint makes sure nothing can ever set it to true. wording_version records the exact consent text the customer saw. evidence_source says whether the customer ticked the boxes themselves or the owner recorded permission for a review received elsewhere. 3. Consent belongs to a version of the text Testimonial text is versioned ( testimonial_versions ), and each consent row points at one version through a foreign key on (testimonial_id, testimonial_version) . Fix a typo or add a translation and you get a new version. The original is kept, and the old consent no longer covers the current text. The dashboard shows "Text changed — needs renewed permission" until a new grant is recorded. 4. Showing it is a query, not a flag The website wall doesn't read a "published" boolean. It asks the database every time: t . status = 'approved' AND c . revoked_at IS NULL AND c . testimonial_version = t . current_version AND c . website_publication c is the latest consent row for that testimonial. Approval is the owner's decision, permission is the customer's, and both have to hold for the current text. Name and role are only included in the feed when name_display is true. Nothing has to be "unpublished" by hand, because the feed is derived from current state. 5. Withdrawal: a hashed token in the URL fragment On submit the customer gets a one-time token ( plwd_… ), shown once and emailed to them if they gave an address. Only its hash is stored ( withdraw_token_hash BYTEA UNIQUE ). The link is /review/withdraw#<token> : the token sits in the fragment, so it never shows up in server logs or referrer headers, and no account is needed. Withdrawing runs one transaction: the testimonial's status becomes revoked every consent row gets revoked_at and revoked_by ( customer , business or deletion ) unsent Social exports are cancelled, and an outbox event tells the Social app to flag drafts already created from it The wall query stops returning it right away. Posts that were already published can't be pulled back automatically, so the business is notified to remove them. What we'd tell someone building the same thing Store each permission separately, with the wording version and where it came from. Tie consent to a version of the text. An edited quote is a new quote. Work out publication from current state at read time instead of keeping a "published" flag you have to remember to update. Make withdrawal work without an account, and keep the token out of logs.
