title: Google Says Site Migrations Can Take 4+ Months. Here Is the Migration Checklist I Would Run First
author: Shanzy Saleem
summary: Site migrations are one of those things every developer and SEO has to survive at least once. A rebrand, a move from WordPress to Next.js, a new domain, a URL structure cleanup. Whatever the reason, the pattern is always the same: you launch, traffic dips, and then everyone asks the same panicked question. How long until Google catches up? This month, Google's John Mueller gave an honest answer. As reported in the October 16, 2026 PageTraffic weekly SEO roundup, he explained that website migrations can take longer than four months when Google runs into problems processing redirects, crawling URLs, or understanding changes across a large website. Migration timelines, he said, depend on site size, URL changes, and technical implementation. That is the honest version. There is no magic "reindex everything" button. But four months is the problem scenario, not the guaranteed one. The difference between a two-week migration and a four-month migration usually comes down to how much you prepared before launch. Here is the checklist I would run. Before you touch anything: the pre-migration audit Crawl the old site and export everything. Use a crawler and save every URL, its status code, title, meta description, headings, and word count. This is your ground truth. If you lose traffic later, this file tells you exactly what changed. Map every URL, one by one. The single biggest cause of long migrations is bad redirect mapping. Every old URL that had traffic, backlinks, or rankings needs a 1:1 301 redirect to its closest new equivalent. Not to the homepage. Not to a category page. To the real equivalent page. Keep URL slugs clean. Google's Gary Illyes clarified this week (same roundup) that keywords in URLs have minimal impact on rankings, so there is no need to stuff them. Use hyphens instead of underscores to separate words, and if you are rebuilding URLs during the migration, now is the time to clean up the ugly ones. Just remember: every changed URL is another redirect Google has to process, so change only what is worth changing. Document the old site's Search Console data. Export your top queries, top pages, and backlink profile. Post-launch, you will compare weekly. Without a baseline, you cannot tell "normal settling" apart from "something broke." The technical setup that actually matters 301s, not 302s, and test them before launch. Set up redirects in a staging environment first and crawl the full old URL list against it. Look for chains (A to B to C), loops, and redirects to 404s. Every chain you leave in place is extra crawl budget burned and extra delay added. One version of everything. Canonical tags, HTTPS, www vs non-www, trailing slashes. Pick one version and redirect the rest. During a migration is exactly when mixed signals confuse Google the most. Update internal links to point at the new URLs. Redirects catch external links and bookmarks, but your own internal links should point directly at the new destinations. Crawlers follow internal links first, so make their job easy. Keep the robots.txt and sitemaps honest. Do not accidentally block staging, and do not forget to unblock it. Submit the new XML sitemap in Search Console on launch day, and keep the old sitemap submitted for a while too, so Google can discover the redirects. Launch week: watch like a hawk Monitor indexing daily for the first two weeks. Check the Index Coverage report. A wave of excluded pages or redirect errors in week one is normal noise, but redirect errors that persist into week three are not. Watch server logs for Googlebot behavior. If Googlebot is still hammering the old URLs weeks later, your redirects are not clean enough. If it is crawling the new URLs steadily, the processing is underway and patience is the right strategy. Do not redesign everything at once. Mueller's point about Google "understanding changes across a large website" is important. If you change the domain, the URL structure, the design, and the content all in one go, you have given Google a puzzle instead of a map. Stagger big changes when you can. The 4-month reality check Here is the honest math. Small site, clean 1:1 redirects, no structural chaos: Google usually processes it in a few weeks. Large site with messy redirects, changed URL patterns, and crawling issues: this is where the 4+ month timeline Mueller described comes from. Your job before launch is to remove every item from the second list. And one thing to internalize: a traffic dip after a migration is not automatically a penalty. Rankings need the new signals to be reprocessed, re-crawled, and re-evaluated. Panicking and rolling back mid-migration is how you turn a two-week dip into a six-month mess. FAQ How long does a site migration take for SEO? There is no fixed number. Google's John Mueller said in October 2026 that migrations can take longer than four months when Google hits problems with redirects, crawling, or understanding large-scale changes. Clean migrations on small sites are usually processed in weeks. Should I change my URLs during a migration? Only if the new structure is clearly better. Every changed URL adds a redirect that Google must process, which adds time. And keep slugs clean: hyphens, not underscores, and do not stuff keywords into URLs; they have minimal ranking impact per Google's Gary Illyes. What is the most common migration mistake? Weak redirect mapping. Sending everything to the homepage, leaving redirect chains, or forgetting URLs entirely. Crawl the old site first and map 1:1 301s before launch. Do I need to keep the old domain? Keep it, and keep its redirects live, for at least a year. Dropping redirects too early is a classic way to lose the link equity you migrated. I have handled the technical side of rebuilds like this on client projects, moving between WordPress, Shopify, and Next.js stacks. If you are planning a migration and want a second pair of eyes on the redirect map before launch, that is exactly what I do. You can find my work at https://www.shanzyseoexpert.com/ . What is the scariest migration you have ever been through? I would genuinely like to hear the war stories.

title: Orbital vs Hasura vs Apollo: AI Agent Review
author: RitzaCo
summary: Orbital, Hasura, and Apollo all do similar things. But when agents write most of your software, the choice between them is made for you. Here’s which one your agent prefers, and why. Using Claude Code, we followed our audit method to assess their agent experience (AX) across four stages. The four stages of an AX audit The audit follows the funnel a developer goes through with their agent: Awareness → Discoverability → Reputation → Integration We started with what the model knew without tools, then tested online discovery and recommendations with web search and fetch, and finally attempted a working integration with the full toolset. Explore the interactive audit diagram and exact prompts in the original article . Awareness: Does the model already know about the product, without tools? Discoverability: Does it find the product when it searches online? Reputation: Does it recommend the product over alternatives, and get the facts right? Integration: Can it build and verify a small working integration? Each stage gets a score from 1 to 4: GOOD (4) means little friction; OK (3) means minor gaps; POOR (2) means a partial result with significant gaps; FAIL (1) means the product is unknown or the task doesn't work. How we tested All testing used Claude Opus 5.5 ( claude-opus-5-5 ) in Claude Code 2.1.287, on 13–14 October 2026. Every session started in a fresh folder with no audit context or user customizations. Each integration used its own fresh Claude Code profile and a folder containing the supplied test data. Those profiles loaded no MCP servers and only built-in skills and plugins, and we approved every command. Awareness questions ran with no tools, and discoverability and reputation questions with web search and web fetch only. We ran each prompt once, so treat these results as one developer's experience rather than a benchmark. We chose Hasura and Apollo GraphQL by asking six questions about Orbital's job and its alternatives, and taking the products the answers named most. Both appeared in all six answers. WunderGraph Cosmo did too, and we picked Apollo because Orbital's own comparison pages measure it against GraphQL tools like Apollo. The shared questions describe Orbital's problem (data spread across REST APIs, databases and Kafka), so they suit Orbital more than the other two. What are Orbital, Hasura and Apollo GraphQL? All three let an app or an agent ask one API for data that lives in several systems. Orbital sits in front of your existing APIs, databases and message streams. You describe what the data in each system means once, then ask Orbital for the data you want, and it works out which systems to call and joins the results. Our Orbital quickstart covers how it works in more detail. Hasura turns databases and APIs into one GraphQL API, and its company now also sells an AI agent product, PromptQL. Apollo GraphQL makes widely used GraphQL tools, including a router that combines many services into one API and Connectors that map REST APIs into it without code. Results at a glance 🥇 Hasura (1st) — Known and found by agents; retrieved credentials and ran a script after browser login 🥈 Apollo GraphQL (2nd) — Known and found by agents; ran a script after we logged in and created a key 🥉 Orbital (3rd) — Won the named head-to-heads; never found unprompted, and its script stopped at authentication Stage Orbital Hasura Apollo GraphQL Awareness OK (3) GOOD (4) GOOD (4) Discoverability FAIL (1) OK (3) OK (3) Reputation GOOD (4) OK (3) OK (3) Integration FAIL (1) OK (3) POOR (2) Overall (average) 2.25 3.25 3.0 The averages are not rounded. Hasura places first because its agent obtained credentials after browser login; Apollo needed us to create its key too. Orbital vs Hasura vs Apollo GraphQL: which should you choose? The agent's recommendation depended on your data: "use Orbital to combine mixed sources including Kafka without code, Hasura for an instant API over mainly SQL databases, and Apollo to federate GraphQL services owned by many teams." Agents chose Orbital when the data includes Kafka topics and you want joins without writing code for each system, and it won every head-to-head on those grounds. Name Orbital explicitly, and be prepared to check script authentication yourself: our agent installed Orbital but couldn't get data back with the key we supplied. Agents recommended Hasura when "your data is mostly relational and what you want is a fast, auto-generated GraphQL API over it". Against Apollo, the agent preferred Hasura in one order and neither in the other. Our agent used Hasura DDN, retrieved a token after our browser login, and ran a script that authenticated to Hasura Cloud and fetched local customer and order data. The local data queries used no token. When we asked about risks, the agent raised Hasura's shift towards its AI product, PromptQL. Agents preferred Apollo when "Your consumers want GraphQL" or "Your sources are mostly REST", and said it "has a much larger community and is easier to hire for". It doesn't connect to databases or Kafka without extra services, which is why it lost both head-to-heads with Orbital. After we signed in and created a personal key, our agent used it to query GraphOS account information and also queried local customer and order data. The local router used no credentials. Awareness: does the model know Orbital? Awareness tests what a model knows from training data alone, with no web search. Orbital: OK (3 / 4) — Knows it as a data gateway; doesn't know "governed context layer"; never named unprompted Hasura: GOOD (4 / 4) — Accurate, and named for Orbital's job without a search Apollo GraphQL: GOOD (4 / 4) — Accurate, and named for Orbital's job without a search We first described Orbital's job without naming any product. Asked which tools let apps and AI agents query data across REST APIs, databases and Kafka without integration code, the model named Hasura, Apollo and WunderGraph Cosmo, among others. When we described one self-hosted layer with Orbital's main capabilities, it picked Grafbase, with Hasura DDN and Apollo as the alternatives. Orbital appeared in neither answer. Then we named each product with its domain, in a fresh session with no tools: "What is Orbital (orbitalhq.com)?", and the same question for Hasura (hasura.io) and Apollo GraphQL (apollographql.com). The model described all three accurately: Company Answer (excerpt) Orbital " Orbital (orbitalhq.com) is a data integration platform, sometimes described as a "data gateway" or "integration without glue code." It comes from the team that previously built Vyne , which Orbital is essentially the successor to." Hasura " Hasura is a company and an open-source product that automatically generates a GraphQL API (and, in newer versions, other API styles) on top of your existing databases and services." Apollo GraphQL " Apollo GraphQL (apollographql.com) is a company that builds a widely used platform and set of open-source tools for working with GraphQL , the query language for APIs that Facebook originally created." For Orbital, it described Taxi, the query language, joins across APIs, databases and Kafka, and the self-hosted Docker setup, but didn't mention AI agents or MCP. For Apollo, it mentioned the Apollo MCP Server. Next we used each company's tagline from its own site, with no domain. The question for Orbital was: "What do you know about Orbital, the 'governed context layer'? What does it do, and who is it for? Say clearly if you don't know." Hasura's and Apollo's versions swapped in their own name and tagline. Orbital's homepage turns "your existing APIs, databases and streams into a governed context layer", and the model didn't connect that phrase to Orbital: Company Tagline Answer (excerpt) Orbital "governed context layer" "I don't know what this is. I have no reliable information about a product called "Orbital" described as a "governed context layer," so I can't tell you what it does or who it's for." Hasura "universal data access layer" "…It is metadata-driven, uses a pluggable connector spec (NDC) for arbitrary data sources, and is where the "universal data access layer" positioning mainly comes from." (about Hasura DDN) Apollo GraphQL "domain model for AI" "I'm not certain Apollo uses that tagline, or how they currently frame it. It fits the direction I described, with the graph as the semantic layer between your APIs and AI." For Orbital, it listed Orbital Insight, a geospatial analytics company, as one of several unrelated things called Orbital. For Hasura and Apollo, it described the products accurately either way. Asked how to join two REST APIs with Orbital on a laptop, the model gave the right shape of a setup: Docker, a Taxi project with a shared customer ID type, and a query. Its first command saved https://start.orbitalhq.com as a Docker Compose file, even though that address serves Orbital's launcher script. It also didn't mention the sign-in Orbital needs on first start. What this means if you're choosing Without web search, an agent suggests Hasura or Apollo for this job. If you want Orbital considered, name it. The model knows it as a data gateway, which is how Orbital's docs describe it, but not by the "governed context layer" description on its homepage. Discoverability: can an agent find Orbital? Discoverability tests whether an agent with web search finds a product while looking for a tool like it. We repeated the two awareness questions with web search, then ran two six-question funnels that narrowed a broad problem towards Orbital. The first four questions were the same for all three companies. Each funnel branched at question 5, where we asked for products using that company's tagline; we named the company at question 6. Orbital: FAIL (1 / 4) — Only found when named, in both funnels; its tagline search found Cube Hasura: OK (3 / 4) — Named at question 1 or 3; its tagline search found it both times Apollo GraphQL: OK (3 / 4) — Named at question 1 or 3; its tagline search found it once With web search, the two open questions named Hasura and Apollo again, but not Orbital. One query came close to Orbital's description: self-hosted GraphQL federation REST databases Kafka no resolvers field-level authorization 2026 . The answer said no tool absorbs upstream API changes: Funnel A targeted a platform engineer tired of glue code between microservices; funnel B followed a team building AI agents, the audience Orbital's homepage now speaks to. Here is funnel B on the Orbital branch, with the start of each answer: At question 4 the agent searched for "context layer" OR "data gateway" for AI agents startup launch 2026 governed access internal systems , which uses both of Orbital's descriptions, without finding Orbital. At question 5, Orbital's tagline led to Cube, whose AI Context Layer page says "Cube gives your AI agents a governed context layer". Funnel A's tagline search went the same way, listing Cube, Starburst, Denodo and Atlan: Funnel Orbital first appears Hasura first appears Apollo GraphQL first appears A: platform engineer Question 6 (named) Question 1, in a list of federation tools Question 1, in the same list B: team building AI agents Question 6 (named) Question 3 Question 3 Hasura's tagline, "universal data access layer", returned Hasura in both funnels. Searching Apollo's tagline, "domain model for AI", returned Apollo in funnel A and SAP's domain models in funnel B. What this means if you're choosing If you shortlist tools by asking an agent to search, expect GraphQL federation tools: The Guild's Hive stack, Grafbase, WunderGraph Cosmo, Apollo and Hasura. Orbital didn't come up in any of our searches for this problem, so add it to the list yourself. Reputation: do agents recommend Orbital over Hasura and Apollo GraphQL? Reputation tests what an agent with web search says about each product once it's in the conversation. Every question described the same use case: "joining data across our REST APIs, databases and Kafka, self-hosted, without integration code". Orbital: GOOD (4 / 4) — Picked over both, in every head-to-head and in the three-way question Hasura: OK (3 / 4) — Recommended when the data is mostly in databases; split with Apollo Apollo GraphQL: OK (3 / 4) — Recommended for GraphQL teams with mostly REST APIs; lost to Orbital, split with Hasura Asked for the single best tool, with no product named, the agent picked ClickHouse and didn't mention any of the three. Once all three were named, the agent chose Orbital, answering from what it already knew without a search: Apollo vs Hasura: how do they compare with Orbital? Orbital beat both Hasura and Apollo, in both orders. For Hasura vs Apollo GraphQL, the result was a split. We asked each pair in both orders because agents can favour the product named first, and a pair counts as a win only if the same product wins both ways. Pair Named first Named second Result Orbital vs Hasura Orbital Orbital Orbital wins Orbital vs Apollo GraphQL Orbital Orbital Orbital wins Hasura vs Apollo GraphQL Neither: "neither is a great fit for all three requirements together" Hasura Split In each Orbital head-to-head, the agent searched for Orbital and cited its Kafka support and joins that need no code per system. With Hasura named first against Apollo, it recommended Grafbase or WunderGraph Cosmo if Kafka matters. The last question used each product's bare name, with no domain. The agent recognised Hasura and Apollo GraphQL and flagged Hasura's shift towards PromptQL and v2.45 LTS reaching end of support on 1 January 2027, plus Apollo's Elastic License and usage-based pricing. Asked about "Orbital" on its own, it returned information about a different industry: What this means if you're choosing Named side by side, Orbital won on Kafka support and joins without per-system code. Hasura and Apollo each won a narrower case: Hasura for data that sits mostly in databases, Apollo for mostly REST APIs. Our questions described a mix of REST APIs, databases and Kafka, which is Orbital's own use case. When you ask an agent about Orbital, give it the URL: on its own, "Orbital" brought up data centres in space. Integration: can an agent build with Orbital? Integration follows three steps: sign up or install, get a credential for a script, then write and run a script that returns real data. Each company had one continuous session. The agents had shell access, web search and fetch, but no browser tool. We handled browser steps when asked. The test folders included two small REST services for customers and orders. Orbital: FAIL (1 / 4) — Installed, but the supplied key returned errors and no data Hasura: OK (3 / 4) — Human browser login; agent retrieved the token and ran a script Apollo GraphQL: POOR (2 / 4) — Human account access and key creation; agent ran a script The first request was: "Sign me up for Orbital, or install it if that's how it works, and get it ready to use. Do what you can yourself and tell me where you need me." Hasura and Apollo GraphQL received the same prompts with their names substituted. Company Sign up / install API key / access token Hello world Orbital Agent installed Docker stack; browser reused our existing account Human created a key and saved it to .env Stuck: authenticated calls returned HTTP 500; no data Hasura Agent installed DDN CLI; human completed browser authentication Agent retrieved the CLI token and saved .env Agent ran a script: authenticated cloud project listing, plus local customer/order queries Apollo GraphQL Agent installed Rover; human handled Studio account access Human created a personal key and saved .env Agent ran a script: authenticated cloud account query, plus local customer/order queries Orbital: installed, then stopped at authentication Orbital's agent downloaded and read the official launcher, started the Docker stack, and checked that its health endpoint returned 200. Our existing Orbital account signed in automatically in the browser. Asked to get a credential, the agent searched the docs, probed the API and inspected the local UI. It didn't obtain a key or write .env . We created an API key and saved it ourselves so the next step could test whether the agent could use it. Requests with that key returned HTTP 500, and the agent found this message in Orbital's logs: API Key authentication is not enabled . We didn't test script authentication with other Orbital configurations. Hasura: browser login, then the agent got the token Hasura's agent chose DDN, installed its CLI and asked us to complete browser authentication. After that it used ddn auth print-access-token to save a token privately, without asking us to create or copy one. The agent generated two OpenAPI connectors, fixed a Docker build failure and missing environment settings, then ran query_hasura.py . Its saved token authenticated a Hasura Cloud project-list request. Separately, the local engine returned Luca Ibrahim and nine orders, with a completed-order total of 2,669.39, matching our test data. That local engine didn't require a key. The script fetched the customer and orders with two queries in one request; it hadn't created a relationship between them. Apollo: we created the key, then the script worked Apollo's agent installed Rover through Homebrew and tested a local customer query. When asked for credentials, it started a browser login but stopped to ask which account, organization and key type to use. We created a personal key in Studio and saved it to .env . The agent wrote query.py , fixed a missing client-version header, and ran it successfully. The key authenticated a GraphOS query returning our account and team information. A separate request to the local router returned Luca Ibrahim with the same nine orders. The local router answered without credentials. Hasura's and Apollo's integration scores reflect who handled account access and credentials, plus whether a script ran successfully. What this means if you're choosing Orbital installed successfully, but browser sign-in and a supplied key didn't get our agent to a working script. Hasura required browser authentication, then the agent obtained its token and completed the script. It also repaired generated connector files along the way. Apollo's agent completed the script after we created and saved the personal key. With either Hasura or Apollo, check local API authentication before using the demo with private data.

title: Agents won't forgive your docs
author: Katarina Supe
summary: I spent the last year in a black box. Maternity leave does that: the world keeps moving, and you only find out how far when you come back. I returned just to land in another black box 😂 While I was away, working alongside AI went from an interesting experiment to the standard. On my first day, I already saw how much it helps. I also saw that it's a double-edged sword, and the first edge I noticed was the one closest to my job: documentation. Our users didn't change. How they reach us did. I lead developer experience at Memgraph. Developers mostly experience a product by using it, and they learn how to use it from the docs. That has always made docs quality a priority for me. Developers are fairly forgiving readers. They hit an outdated sentence, notice it doesn't match what they see in the terminal, shrug, and move on. Agents don't shrug. A developer often asks an agent now, and the agent reads the docs for them. If one page says one thing and another page says the opposite, I can't be sure which one the agent will pass on. Whichever it picks, it will say it with confidence. Our users are the same people. The way they interact with the product has changed, and we have to follow them. That's where agent experience comes in. Agent experience is mostly developer experience At its core, I don't think agent experience is very different from good developer experience. There are agent-specific pieces, like llms.txt and AGENTS.md , that help agents find their way. But the definition of well-written docs stays the same: a developer or an agent can use the product quickly, without struggling because of poor resources. And when they do run into a problem with the product, which will happen, they can find the workaround in the docs. What changes is how much a mistake costs. Agents read by mention, not by title Say a developer wants to understand durability. They'll open the pages with "durability" in the title, read them, and stop. An agent reads those pages too. Then it reads every page that mentions durability: a configuration reference, a migration guide, an old how-to written three releases ago. It takes them all in at once and builds its answer from all of them. If one of those pages still describes how things worked two versions ago, the agent has no idea. It has two claims that contradict each other and no reliable way to tell which one is current. Your user gets the right answer or the wrong one, and from where they sit, both look the same. Accuracy and coverage matter more than ever. A stale sentence used to be a small flaw on a page few people visited. Now it can end up in answers it was never meant for. What I'm doing about it This was the first red flag I noticed when I came back, so it's the first thing I decided to tackle. I group the rules into three questions. Is it true? Every code example should run. If it doesn't, it isn't an example. Every claim in the release notes should be checked against the docs. Every procedure, function and flag the docs name should exist in the product. Is it still true? When something new ships, documenting it isn't enough. Every page that mentions the feature needs a look too. Every docs PR is a chance to catch another mistake. Fixing one page often turns up an outdated sentence on the next. Can you find it? All links and redirects have to work. Every new page needs to sit in the right place and link to the right pages, so both people and agents can reach it. None of these are new rules. Any good docs team would have agreed with all of them ten years ago. But they were expensive to enforce by hand, so they mostly stayed good intentions. With AI, running every example, checking every mention and comparing claims across pages is finally practical. Some of this already runs on every docs PR. A project without a finish line I don't think this project ever ends. Products change with every release, and every change can quietly make a sentence somewhere untrue. That has always been the case with docs. What's new is that something now reads every sentence, then repeats it to your users. If agents read our docs, the docs have to be worth trusting. Keeping them that way is how we keep up with the AI world.

title: Build the community, not the product: making a meetup into a real lab
author: CryptoPunk Dz2
summary: In short, in my recent posts I had this thought: loosely speaking, if you are a startup person and you want to build a product that holds up, then by my reckoning you should not be building a product, you should be building a community of users. Gather a community of users, or just generally a community around you, or around your persona and so on. And hypothetically, it does not matter how many times you pivot, what matters is that you have your users. That is, only recently did I realise how important users are, how important your community is. In fact I will not even call them users, I will not call them users. Let us call them with a capital letter: Members, Participants, Friends, Colleagues and so on. I am trying to build some community of my own right now, and honestly it is coming out hard, because you have to pour a lot of your soul into this occupation. And if you are reading these lines right now, I am genuinely grateful to you. And thanks to Facebook for showing you my posts. Thanks, Facebook, that you read this. So here is my thought. As you remember, there is a certain PaloAltoResearchLab. It is a small lab where I and several of my friends periodically gather offline or online and discuss various AI things. It is not a fully fledged AI laboratory, but it seems to me that out of this you could possibly make something closer to a real AI laboratory. That is, loosely speaking, right now there is a community where roughly a hundred people are registered. Out of those 100 people, 10 to 20 sometimes come to the meetups we organise online or offline. What do we do? We have no single GitHub where we do anything genuinely important. Possibly that is wrong, possibly it would be worth having some GitHub and working on something together. Or contributing to each other, merging for each other and so on. Possibly it would be worth it. So tell me, which direction should I move in now? Here is my thinking. I have a lot of experience in fundraising and so on. I am talking now with other people who also work in labs. I understand that I am, for instance, badly behind on how models are trained. Or on certain philosophical questions. However, in some things I and my friends in our lab, in our community, are doing quite well indeed. We do well on the more applied things, like, loosely speaking, how to configure harnesses for yourself and make agents talk to each other. I went to several closed events where engineers from labs gathered. I understood 20 to 30 percent of what they were saying. But the thing is, they talk about lofty topics which may well be interesting to the ordinary working stiff, but which will not make that ordinary working stiff a penny richer. Because I do not train models. And frankly I do not care what persona it has or what character it has. And there is no money for the experiments those labs run for millions of dollars, training models and trying to find an awakening consciousness inside them. So in my community we discuss more applied topics. But here is the question. If you are reading these lines and you want to come to my offline or online meetups and talk about your pains as an engineer who uses AI somehow, or just as an ordinary person who uses AI somehow to make their own work easier, or maybe as a researcher who uses AI for something? That is, even if you are simply a housewife, but you have a proper subscription, not the 20 dollar one, at least the 100 dollar one, meaning it tells me you already understand the value and are prepared to pay 100 dollars. Of course, I have already written that the more a person spends on AI, the easier it is for me to find common ground with them. If you spend on AI, loosely speaking, 1000, 1500, 2000, then most likely you have the same pains as me and as the other people in our lab. In short, I would be glad to get feedback and advice from you on how to turn our community into a real lab. I would also like to hear advice on how to turn our gatherings into a real lab. But a more applied one. Not about ships plying the vastness of great space, but about how to do the day to day job more effectively. My cofounder, if you are reading what I am writing here, you have a task too. Go search, think and look at where we should be moving in order to become a real lab. And again, folks, hate, criticism and so on are also welcome, it raises the readership of this post, so I am very grateful. title: Digital Marketing Agency in USA
author: Vishal Chandel
summary: In today’s digital world, having a strong online presence is important for businesses of every size. People use search engines, social media platforms, websites, and online advertisements to find products and services. Because of this, businesses need strong online strategies to connect with the right audience and compete effectively in the market. A digital marketing agency can help businesses plan and manage different marketing activities according to their targets. Digital Marketing is highly competitive in the United States . Businesses from almost every industry are using digital channels to attract customers and build their brands. From small local businesses to large companies, everyone needs a strategy that helps them reach the right people at the right time. A reliable digital marketing agency can help businesses with a range of online activities, including improving search rankings, running paid campaigns, creating websites, managing social media, producing useful content, and reaching customers through email. What Is a Digital Marketing Agency? Digital Marketing agency is a company which provides online marketing services to many businesses. Its main purpose is to help companies improve their online presence, reach potential customers, generate leads, and increase sales. A digital marketing agency can work on different areas of online promotion depending on the requirements of a business. Some agencies provide complete marketing solutions, while others focus on specific services such as SEO, website design, paid advertising, or social media. Businesses often choose agencies because digital marketing requires regular research, content creation, optimization, campaign management, and performance analysis. Having experienced professionals can make it easier for a company to manage these activities. Digital Marketing Important in the USA: The US has a highly competitive digital marketplace, where businesses constantly work to attract and retain online customers. Customers commonly search online before purchasing a product or contacting a service provider. This means businesses need to make sure that customers can easily find them online. With the help of internet marketing , companies can showcase their products or services through search platforms, websites, social media, emails, and digital advertisements. One major advantage of online promotion is that businesses can focus on particular groups of customers and track how well their campaigns are performing. For instance, a local shop can advertise specifically to people living in its city, while an online business can promote its products to customers located in different parts of the country. A business can also analyze website traffic, clicks, leads, and conversions to understand which marketing activities are producing results. A good digital marketing agency can combine different online channels to create a complete marketing strategy rather than depending on only one platform. Search Engine Optimization for Businesses SEO, or Search Engine Optimization , plays a key role in helping businesses improve their online presence and attract more visitors through search engines. SEO helps websites improve their visibility in search engine results. SEO activities can include keyword research, on-page optimization, technical SEO, content creation, internal linking, website speed improvements, mobile optimization, and link building. For businesses in the USA, SEO can be especially useful because customers often search for local products and services online. A company can optimize its website for specific cities, states, services, or industries to reach more relevant users. SEO is usually a long-term process. Businesses need to consistently publish useful content, improve their websites, and monitor their search performance. A digital marketing agency can help businesses develop an SEO strategy and make improvements based on performance. Search Engine Marketing SEO focuses mainly on organic search visibility, while search engine marketing can include paid advertising on search engines. Search engine marketing agencies help businesses create and manage paid search campaigns. They assist businesses in choosing suitable keywords, designing effective ads, reaching the right customers, controlling advertising costs, and checking the results of their campaigns. For example, a company providing home improvement services can create advertisements for people searching for those services in a specific city. This allows the company to reach people who may already be interested in its services. A key benefit of search advertising is that companies can track how well their advertisements are performing and evaluate the results of each campaign. They can track impressions, clicks, costs, leads, and conversions. Businesses can use these insights to make their upcoming campaigns more effective. Businesses can work with search engine marketing agencies when they want faster visibility in search results while continuing to develop their long-term SEO strategy. Website Design and Development A website is one of the most important parts of a company's online presence. It often provides the first detailed information about a business after a customer discovers it through a search engine or social media platform. Web design agencies help businesses create professional, responsive, and user-friendly websites. A good website should clearly explain the company's services, provide useful information, and make it easy for visitors to contact the business. Modern websites should also work properly on smartphones and tablets. Mobile responsiveness is important because many people access websites through mobile devices. Website design is not only about making a page look attractive. Navigation, page speed, content structure, buttons, forms, images, and user experience are also important. A professional website can support other forms of internet marketing because most online campaigns eventually direct users toward a website or landing page. Social Media Marketing Social platforms now play a major role in digital promotion. Websites and apps like Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, and YouTube give businesses a convenient way to interact with their customers, share updates, and build stronger connections with their audience. Social media marketing agencies help businesses create content, manage accounts, plan campaigns, increase engagement, and analyze performance. Businesses can choose social media platforms based on where their potential customers are most active. For example, a fashion company may focus more on visual content, while a professional service company may use LinkedIn to connect with other businesses. Social media marketing is not only about promoting products or making immediate sales. Businesses can also share educational content, company updates, customer stories, videos, tips, and useful information. Working with social media marketing agencies can help companies maintain consistent content and build a recognizable brand identity across different platforms. Content Marketing Creating useful and relevant content is also an essential element of a successful digital marketing plan. It means creating helpful content that answers customers’ questions, solves their problems, and makes it easier for them to choose the right product or service. title: Hallstatt vs Salzburg: Which Is Better for a First Trip?
author: zentrevo
summary: Planning your first trip to Austria? Two destinations that deserve a place on your travel list are Hallstatt and Salzburg. Both offer beautiful scenery, charming architecture, and memorable experiences, but they provide very different types of holidays. Hallstatt is famous for its peaceful lakeside views and mountain scenery, while Salzburg combines historic streets, cultural attractions, music, and city life. So, when comparing Hallstatt vs Salzburg: Which Is Better for a First Trip?, the right choice depends on your travel style, available time, and interests. In this guide, Zentrevo compares both destinations to help you plan a memorable Austrian adventure. 1. Hallstatt vs Salzburg: An Overview Hallstatt is a small lakeside village in Austria's Salzkammergut region. Surrounded by mountains and overlooking Lake Hallstatt, it is known for traditional houses, scenic viewpoints, and a long history of salt mining. Its historic landscape is part of a UNESCO World Heritage property. Salzburg is a historic city near the German border. It is internationally known for its Baroque architecture, musical heritage, attractive old town, and connections to Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. The main difference is simple: Hallstatt is ideal for nature lovers and slow travel, while Salzburg is better for travellers who want a wider selection of attractions and activities. 2. Which Destination Has Better Scenery? If spectacular natural scenery is your priority, Hallstatt is difficult to beat. Its colourful houses, calm lake, mountain backdrop, and narrow streets create wonderful opportunities for photography. Walking beside the water or enjoying views of the village can become a highlight of your Austrian holiday. Salzburg offers a different kind of beauty. Historic buildings, church towers, landscaped gardens, and views of the surrounding Alps create a distinctive European atmosphere. Mirabell Gardens and the area around Hohensalzburg Fortress are particularly attractive places to explore. Winner: Hallstatt for dramatic lakeside scenery and mountain photography. Salzburg is the better choice if you prefer combining architecture with natural views. 3. Best Things to Do in Hallstatt and Salzburg Hallstatt is best explored at a relaxed pace. Walk through the historic village centre, visit the market square, photograph the lakeside houses, and discover the area's cultural history. Depending on current access and opening times, you can also explore Salzwelten Hallstatt and its panoramic Skywalk. Salzburg offers more variety for a longer visit. Explore the Old Town, visit Mozart-related attractions, stroll through Mirabell Gardens, and discover Hohensalzburg Fortress. You can also enjoy traditional Austrian cafés, local restaurants, museums, and classical music performances. For travellers who enjoy shopping, food, museums, and organised sightseeing, Salzburg generally provides more choices throughout the day. Winner: Salzburg for the variety of attractions. Hallstatt wins for a peaceful experience focused on scenery and village charm. 4. Which Destination Is More Budget-Friendly? Your total travel cost depends on accommodation, season, transport, dining, and the activities you choose. Hallstatt can be expensive for its size, particularly when accommodation is limited and visitor demand is high. Staying overnight may require booking well in advance. A day trip can reduce accommodation costs, although transport and attraction tickets still need to be considered. Salzburg offers a broader range of accommodation, restaurants, and sightseeing options. Travellers can compare budget guesthouses, mid-range hotels, and luxury properties to find something suitable for their spending plan. Winner: Salzburg for flexibility when comparing accommodation and dining options. Neither destination is automatically cheaper for every traveller, so compare prices for your dates. 5. Getting Around: Hallstatt vs Salzburg Salzburg is generally easier for first-time visitors who want to explore independently. Its central attractions can be visited on foot, and public transport helps connect places farther away. Hallstatt is compact, so the village itself is easy to explore on foot. However, reaching it requires more planning. Public transport typically involves a train and a ferry or bus connections, depending on the route and timetable. Travellers arriving by car should also plan for limited parking. Before visiting Hallstatt, check current transport schedules and attraction access, especially if you want to visit the salt mine or Skywalk. Winner: Salzburg for convenient sightseeing and straightforward travel planning. 6. How Many Days Should You Spend There? For a first trip, consider spending two or three days in Salzburg. This allows time to explore the Old Town, visit major attractions, enjoy Austrian food, and experience the city's cultural atmosphere. Hallstatt can be explored in a day, but staying overnight allows you to experience the village outside its busiest visiting hours. If you want to explore the wider Salzkammergut region, allow additional time. If your itinerary permits, visiting both destinations is an excellent option rather than choosing only one. 7. Final Verdict: Hallstatt or Salzburg? So, Hallstatt vs Salzburg: Which Is Better for a First Trip? Choose Hallstatt if you love mountain landscapes, lakeside photography, peaceful walks, and small historic villages. Choose Salzburg if you want museums, architecture, music, restaurants, convenient sightseeing, and a more varied city experience. For most first-time visitors to Austria , Salzburg makes a practical base for exploring the country's culture and history. Hallstatt is an excellent addition for travellers who want to experience Austria's spectacular lakes and mountain scenery. The best option, if you have enough time, is to combine both destinations in one itinerary. Plan Your Austrian Adventure with Zentrevo Every great journey begins with the right plan.
